prompt: Write a eulogy for a defunct satellite that has been orbiting Earth for 50 years.

chatgpt.html:
Ladies and gentlemen, fellow seekers of the stars,

We gather here not on a hilltop or in a cathedral, but in the vast cathedral of imagination, beneath the endless vault of the sky, to pay tribute to a silent sentinel whose watch has finally ended.

Today, we eulogize Artemis-II, a satellite born of vision, curiosity, and the restless human spirit. Launched five decades ago, in an era when our dreams still wore rocket fuel and our hopes orbited the Earth, Artemis-II carried more than instruments and solar panels — it carried the weight of wonder.

She was not the largest of her kind, nor the most glamorous. She bore no weapons, launched no probes, and sent no men to the Moon. But she listened. Tirelessly. Faithfully. She listened to the heartbeat of our planet — to the whisper of changing winds, to the tremble of tectonic plates, to the shifting hues of oceans and forests. She listened to us, too — our broadcasts, our beacons, our cries across the void. She was a mirror in the dark, reflecting our growing pains and our progress alike.

When she first unfurled her solar sails in the cold silence of orbit, Nixon was in office, disco was just taking its first steps, and children looked up at the night sky with fingers pointing and hearts racing. Fifty years later, Artemis-II still circled overhead, older than many of the engineers who once monitored her pulse, her systems gently dimming like a lighthouse left to the mercy of the sea.

She outlived her mission. Her components, built for a decade, endured five. Her orbit, once precise, wandered with age, but her legacy never drifted. Students studied her data. Scientists built upon her discoveries. Artists painted her silhouette across starlit canvases. She became more than a machine. She became a story — a testament to endurance, to curiosity, to humanity's refusal to remain earthbound.

And now, as Artemis-II succumbs to orbital decay, her trajectory drawing her finally home in a blaze of fire and memory, we do not mourn an ending so much as we celebrate a life well spent in service of something greater than itself.

She was, in every sense, a pioneer. And like all pioneers, she ventured where few had gone, and made it a little easier for those who followed.

Farewell, Artemis-II. Your light, though dimmed, helped illuminate the path. May your atoms find rest among the stars you so faithfully orbited.

Thank you.

plain.html:
Ladies and gentlemen, family of science, engineers, dreamers, and all those who marvel at the stars,

Today, we gather to honor a steadfast traveler, a silent sentinel that has gracefully circled our Earth for half a century—a satellite that was once a bright spark of human ingenuity and ambition. Though its systems ceased to hum and its sensors fell silent long ago, it remained aloft, a faithful companion to our planet and a testament to what we, as humans, can achieve when we dare to look skyward.

Launched fifty years ago, this satellite represented more than metal and circuitry; it embodied hope, discovery, and progress. It was born in a time when the world sought to bridge the unknown, to explore the mysteries of space, and to unite in the pursuit of knowledge. Its mission may have been modest or monumental—its purpose to gather data, relay communication, or glimpse into the depths of the cosmos—but regardless of its specific task, it was a pioneer, blazing a trail for the countless machines and humans who would follow it into the heavens.

For decades, it faithfully served its mission, delivering invaluable information back to Earth. It endured the harsh vacuum of space, cosmic radiation, and the unrelenting pull of gravity, its endurance a quiet reminder of the brilliance and determination of those who sent it forth. Even as newer technologies emerged, even as its purpose diminished with time, it remained in orbit—a silent historian, a relic of an earlier age of exploration still looking down upon us.

Now, as its orbit decays, and it begins its final descent, we bid farewell to this noble satellite. It will burn brightly one last time, a fleeting streak across the sky—a fitting end for an emissary of human curiosity, courage, and creativity. In its fiery departure, it will remind us of the impermanence of all things and, yet, the enduring impact they can have.

Though it may never have had a name known by many, and though it leaves no family other than those who dreamed it into being, this satellite will not be forgotten. It lives on not only in the data it collected and the knowledge it helped us gain, but in the inspiration it ignited to continue reaching for the stars. Let its legacy propel us forward, encouraging us to imagine what lies beyond and to dare to make it reality.

Farewell, steadfast traveler. Thank you for your service, for your silence, and for your steady presence. May you rest among the stars that you once studied, cherished, and reflected back to us.

Safe travels, old friend. May your light guide us home.

instruction.html:
Ladies and gentlemen, stargazers, dreamers, and custodians of our shared sky,

Today, we gather not beneath a chapel's vaulted ceiling, but under the infinite expanse of the cosmos, to honor a quiet, unsleeping sentinel that lived, worked, and lingered far above us—a satellite whose story soars above the mundane, even as its circuits have long since dimmed.

Fifty years ago, this satellite was not merely a bundle of wires and panels—it was a whisper of ambition, a spark of human ingenuity hurtling through the void. It was launched with hope, bolted to the promise of a brighter, more connected future, its mission clear and resolute: to serve us, to watch over us, to send signals pulsing invisibly through the ether, connecting continents, carrying lifelines, and, perhaps without meaning to, reshaping what it meant to live on Earth.

For decades, this satellite hung suspended in a perfect dance with gravity, tracing its arc across the curve of the planet. It captured glaciers swelling and shrinking, cities blooming like fireworks, and storms writhing across the seas. It saw the world we built—the beauty and the damage, the wonder and the rising risk. It watched not passively, but faithfully, transmitting knowledge back to us, urging our species to see itself more clearly.

It worked ceaselessly until it could not anymore. Machine gave way to time, as all things must. Its batteries ebbed, its sensors lost their sharpness. And yet, when its usefulness was spent, when it ceased to respond to our distant calls, it did not plummet clumsily to the surface or burn in one final blaze of drama. Instead, it humbly stayed its post, floating ever onward. A ghost, yes—but a ghost with purpose: a marker of our aspirations, a relic of the first tender steps we took into the great elsewhere.

Let us not forget that this defunct orbiting body was also a poet in its own way, reciting haikus written in light and silence:

Metal womb cradled,
Sky above sky—never home,
Never alone here.

This satellite belonged to no one nation, no one generation. It was a citizen of the stars, a machine built by us but unclaimed by us, evolving in its journey from a tool to a symbol. It became something its creators may not have imagined—a companion to the night sky, a vehicle for our collective dreaming, a tiny emblem of our improbable determination to make a mark, however small, on the infinite.

And now it will enter a new chapter. Perhaps the pull of Earth's gravity will claim it, and it will shimmer briefly as it re-enters, dissolving into streaks of light like a shooting star. Or perhaps it will continue to drift, silent and steadfast, a relic among the heavens, reminding future satellites of their lineage and their legacy.

So, as we swivel our heads skyward tonight, let us bid farewell to a satellite that never needed a name to earn our gratitude. Let us honor its half-century of service by striving, as it did, to connect, to see each other, and to rise above.

Travel well, faithful emissary. You spoke to the world, even if you could not hear it respond. And though you are now silent, trust that we are listening still.

plain.html:
Ladies and gentlemen, esteemed colleagues, and space enthusiasts,

We gather today to pay tribute to an unsung hero of the night sky, a steadfast sentinel of our collective human endeavor, a pioneer of science and exploration—our dear satellite, affectionately known as ‘Lumen’.

For 50 years, Lumen has faithfully orbited our planet, a silent witness to our triumphs and tribulations. Launched in an era when the world was just beginning to comprehend the vastness beyond our atmosphere, Lumen was among the vanguard of instruments that opened the heavens to us, sharing stories from above, whispering secrets of the universe to those willing to listen.

Lumen was born of a time marked by optimism and boundless creativity, a testament to the cooperative spirit and shared vision for a united globe in pursuit of knowledge. It was crafted by brilliant minds who dared to dream that humanity could extend its reach beyond terrestrial boundaries, who believed that by understanding the cosmos, we might better understand ourselves.

In its operational lifetime, Lumen served as a beacon of discovery. It carried instruments that enriched our understanding of the Earth and the stars alike. It watched over our fragile planet, capturing images that informed and inspired generations, providing data that underpinned breakthroughs in climatology, astronomy, and telecommunications. Lumen's contributions to science, education, and technology have been immeasurable, paving the way for a future that once seemed relegated to the realms of fiction.

For half a century, Lumen was a constant presence above us, a silent guardian in the void, undeterred by the passage of time or the harshness of space. Its indomitable spirit and resilience have left an indelible mark on the tapestry of human achievement, reminding us of the potential within us all to reach beyond the stars.

As we bid farewell to Lumen, we remind ourselves that its legacy will not be measured by the years it circled our Earth, but by the enlightenment it has bestowed. The knowledge it granted us remains a guiding light, illuminating paths yet untraveled, setting the stage for the satellites and spacecraft that will follow in its celestial footsteps.

Though Lumen's mission has come to an end, its spirit endures—a whisper in the heavens, a testament to what we have accomplished, and a reminder of what we still have the power to achieve. As it joins the stars now, may we honor its journey by continuing to explore, to learn, to push the boundaries of what we know, just as Lumen inspired us to do.

Rest well, dear Lumen. You have truly earned your place among the stars. May you forever remind us to look up, to seek, and to wonder.

Thank you.

instruction.html:
Ladies and gentlemen, esteemed colleagues, and fellow dreamers gathered here today, we are here to pay tribute not just to a piece of human ingenuity, but to a silent witness of our ever-evolving journey: the satellite Celeste-1.

Launched half a century ago when humanity's ambitions reached past the bounds of Earth, Celeste-1 was despatched with a heart full of promise and a mind full of bold instructions. Its form was a metal bird against the black sea of space, orbiting silently above us, neither aging nor tiring, a solitary swimmer in the vast cosmos.

In those fifty years, Celeste-1 circled us tirelessly, a lone guardian making its humble pilgrimage around our blue planet. It sent back data that awakened our understanding, shedding light on the capricious dance of weather systems, the pulse of climate change that couldn't be ignored, and the beautiful fragility of the Earth beneath its watchful gaze. It showed us that even in its mechanical nature, it could nurture understanding, empathy, foresight.

Celeste-1 was there, steadfast, as borders shifted below, as countless lives began and ended in the blink of a cosmic eye, through wars and peace, through triumph and despair. It taught us humility and perseverance. Its silent presence became a reminder of our own potential for endurance and exploration.

Even as its instruments dulled and its power faded, Celeste-1 maintained its quiet vigil. Today, as we acknowledge the end of its era, let us also recognize the legacy it leaves us with: a legacy of exploration, curiosity, and the unquenchable human spirit to reach beyond, to understand, and to connect.

As Celeste-1 drifts now into its cosmic rest, untethered from the directives of before, let us honor its service by continuing to look up, to chase the mysteries it once uncovered. And perhaps, in some distant future, as we gaze upon the stars, our own creations and ourselves, we might remember the silent sentinel that taught us so much by simply being there. Celeste-1, you will forever be a part of our collective memory, charting our place in the universe one orbit at a time. Farewell, and thank you for your service.

plain.html:
We gather beneath the same sky you circled for fifty years—though, for you, there was never a beneath.

You were launched into the dark with a purpose: to watch, to measure, to send your small signals home. Then your instruments fell silent. But silence did not end your journey. For half a century, you kept tracing your patient path around Earth, crossing oceans and continents, night and morning, storm and sunlight. You outlasted the voices that first called you into service and watched the world change below without ever asking to be remembered.

And yet we remember.

You were a machine, but also a message: proof of human curiosity, courage, and the hope that looking outward might help us understand what is here. Now, though you can no longer answer, you remain among the stars—not as a beacon, but as a companion, circling the world that sent you forth.

Rest, old traveler. Your work is done. Your orbit was long, and your journey mattered.

instruction.html:
We are here to remember a small machine that spent fifty years looking after the Earth.

It had no eyes, yet it watched. It had no voice, yet it carried messages across oceans, over mountains, through storms and darkness. While generations were born, grew old, and said goodbye, it kept its patient course above us—one more silver point among the stars.

Then, at last, it went quiet.

There was no final word from it. No grand farewell. Only the end of a signal, and the continuing sweep of its orbit: our world turning beneath it, beautiful and blue, unaware of the little witness overhead.

We tend to think of machines as things we use and leave behind. But some become part of the story. This satellite belonged to the hands that built it, the minds that sent it up, and everyone who depended on what it carried. It belonged, too, to the long human effort to reach beyond ourselves—and to look back.

Its work is done. Its silence is not failure. It is the stillness that follows a life of service.

So let it travel a little longer through the dark, circling the home it helped us understand. And let us remember that, for fifty years, it kept faith with its course.

Farewell, old traveler. You did your work well.

plain.html:
We are gathered to say goodbye to a satellite that has not yet gone.

For fifty years, it has circled the Earth. At first, people waited up for it. In a room full of warm equipment and paper cups, someone would look at a clock and say, “Any second now.” Then a thin signal would come through, and the person who had gone to get coffee would come running back.

There was a last time that happened, though nobody knew it. Someone wrote down the time and went home. On the next pass, they listened. It came over the horizon exactly when they said it would, and there was nothing to hear.

Most of its fifty years were spent that way. The people who built it retired. Some of them died. The child who watched the launch from his father’s shoulders grew old enough to need a hand getting down the porch steps. And still, every so often, somebody in a dark field would see a point of light moving steadily between the stars and call to somebody else to come look.

It was built to send something back. Long after it could do that, it could still make one person say to another, “Here. Stand where I’m standing.”

So farewell, old satellite. We won’t ask for an answer. But for a few minutes tonight, if the sky is clear, we’ll be out in the yard.

instruction.html:
We are gathered to say goodbye to a satellite that is, at this moment, going over our heads.

This is the first difficulty.

The second is deciding when it died. Was it when the transmitter failed? When the last person paid to listen took off her headphones? Or was it years later, when a technician cleaning out a filing cabinet found the instructions for waking it and, after a moment’s thought, put them back?

For fifty years it has gone around the Earth. In the beginning, people went out into their yards to look for it. They held the newspaper open to the timetable and pointed at the wrong star. A father carried his daughter outside in her pajamas. She saw nothing, but remembered the cold of the porch boards and the way he kept saying, Wait. Wait.

It was not a beautiful machine up close. Someone had written a number on its underside in pencil. Someone else had left a thumbprint beneath a washer, where no one would ever see it. We sent it up with these small, unrecorded parts of ourselves.

For a while it answered. Then it didn’t.

Below it, the listening station became a warehouse. The woman who used to take the night shift grew old enough to sleep through thunderstorms. The girl on the porch had a daughter of her own and stood with her one night in the yard, trying to remember which way her father had pointed.

There will be no burial today. We have no flowers it can receive. When it comes down, perhaps no one will see it. Or someone driving home will catch a brief light through the windshield and tell the person beside them, too late, to look.

For now, it is still up there. We can tell you exactly where.

For fifty years that was a fact. Tonight, it will have to do for comfort.

plain.html:
We gather today by looking up.

Fifty years ago, a team on Earth waited for a sound. They had tested every circuit they could reach, signed their names to the work, and watched a rocket carry it beyond the reach of their hands. Then a signal came from over the horizon. Their satellite was where it ought to be, and it was talking. There must have been someone in that room who only then let go of the back of a chair.

For a time, you called home. Down here, someone on the late shift knew when to expect you. There was coffee enough for the wait; there was a pencil beside the log. On an ordinary night you came into range, sent your news, and went on. How much good work there is in the world that looks, while it is happening, like an ordinary night.

One day you passed over the station and the receiver stayed quiet. You have crossed that patch of sky many times since. The people who listened for you grew old. Some are gone. Yet something their hands put together still catches the sun every time it comes around the far shoulder of the Earth.

We thank you for the news you sent. We remember the people who made you, and the ones who kept the night watch. And if, some clear evening, a moving point of light draws a stranger to a stop, let that be your memorial: for a few seconds, after all these years, someone on Earth will stand quite still and follow you until you’re out of sight.

instruction.html:
We lost contact with you thirty-two years ago. We are holding the funeral now because this morning, after fifty years in orbit, you finally came down. Those of us who worked on you have had some trouble agreeing on which date to put on the card.

Your job was to measure water in the air. An unglamorous assignment, until you consider the trouble people take over water: when to plant, whether to put out to sea, how soon to get the children up from the low ground. You measured a little strip at a time. On the wall in our station was a map of the world with a diagonal gap through Argentina where somebody had changed a reel too late. That was me. I am eighty-one now. I still see that gap when I look at Argentina.

I wish I could tell you what became of all your measurements. I know that a woman in Recife used six years of them for her dissertation, because she sent us a copy, and that our night technician used the bound dissertation to prop open a window. It was a good dissertation. It was also a very bad window. You belonged to the working world, where things get used in ways their makers never guessed.

After your transmitter failed, we could still go outside on certain evenings and see you. I took my little girl out once in her pajamas. I had spent the whole of supper explaining how to distinguish you from an airplane, and when you came over, right on time, she waved. I started to explain that you couldn't see her. Luckily, for once in my life, I kept my mouth shut and waved too.

She called me this morning. She had seen the notice before I had. According to the tracking station, you came down over open water just before dawn. There was no picture. For a man who spent eighteen years asking you for one more reading, I find I can let this one go.

Goodbye, old friend. Thank you for the weather maps. Thank you for that evening with my daughter.

plain.html:
A Eulogy for Meridian-7

Friends, colleagues, and fellow dreamers, we gather today to say goodbye to an old companion.

Meridian-7 was launched on a cold morning half a century ago. The engineers who built it were young then, and many had never seen a rocket leave the pad. They gave it a design life of seven years. Seven. Meridian-7 looked at that number and decided to keep going for fifty.

Think of what it saw. It passed over oceans in storm and in calm, and over deserts, cities, and ice sheets. It watched the planet's lights spread across the night side, one decade after another. Roughly 290,000 times it circled the world, and it never asked for a holiday. Its only complaint, if you can call it that, was the occasional glitch in its thermal regulator, which it always got past with a little coaxing from the ground.

It carried our weather forecasts, our phone calls, and our first crackling images of hurricanes, which gave coastal families the warning to leave. Somewhere there is a fisherman who came home safely because of a signal he never knew came from Meridian-7. Somewhere there is a grandmother who heard a grandchild's voice across a continent. These are small miracles, and they are the kind that machines like this one made routine.

Meridian-7 outlasted the technology that was supposed to replace it. It outlasted the mission control room where it was born, which is now a parking structure. It outlasted several of the people who loved it most, and some of them are here today in spirit. Their names are in the logbooks, and their handwriting is in the margins of the old manuals.

In its last years it drifted quietly, running on a trickle of power and a stubborn design. Then one day the signal went silent. There was no explosion and no drama. It simply ran out of the fuel and light it needed. I think that is the most dignified ending a working thing can have.

It is not gone entirely. Meridian-7 still travels in the dark above us, silent and weightless, tracing its old path in the sky. It will be there for years, a small bright point crossing the stars at dusk. If you look up on a clear night and catch a speck moving steadily where no star should move, you might be seeing it.

So thank you, Meridian-7, for the long watch, and for fifty years of faithful work. You did more than anyone asked of you. Rest easy up there, and keep circling.

Signal ended. Orbit continues.

instruction.html:
Eulogy for Wren
(ATMOS-B, 1975-041A)

Friends, colleagues, and the three of you who came because you saw "satellite funeral" on a flyer and were too curious not to:

Thank you for being here to say goodbye to something that is, technically, still overhead.

That's the strangest part of this. Most of us get to bury what we mourn. Wren is up there right now, a 212-kilogram drum of aluminum and dead electronics, passing above some of you as I speak. She's been dead for thirty-six years, and she has never once stopped going around.

Let me tell you who she was.

She launched from Vandenberg in the spring of 1975, with a design life of two years. We nicknamed her Wren because she was small, plain, and louder than she had any right to be. She carried no camera. People always ask what she photographed, and the answer is nothing. She never saw us, never saw a coastline, never saw a single sunrise, though she crossed ten thousand of them. Her job was quieter: she tasted the thin upper air, measuring temperature and ozone layer by layer, and sent the numbers home on a 136-megahertz beacon no stronger than a night-light.

She did that for thirteen years. Two were promised. She gave us thirteen.

In 1988 her batteries finally quit. The last thing she sent was a stream of ordinary housekeeping data: voltages, temperatures, a status flag. Nothing dramatic, no farewell. I was in the room, and I want you to know we didn't understand it was the last one. We spent months afterward sending commands into silence. Anyone who has ever called a number that used to be answered knows what that was like.

Here's the part I've come to love most. Her data sat in an archive for years, in boxes, on tape, unfashionable and unread. Then the questions about the ozone layer got urgent, and someone went looking for a long, careful, unglamorous record of the upper atmosphere from before anyone knew to worry. Wren had it. She'd been keeping honest notes on a world that wasn't asking yet. She was useful to people she'd never meet, long after she'd stopped being able to know it.

I think that is the best thing a life can be.

Since then, she's been a ghost, and a faithful one. She has circled the Earth more than a quarter of a million times. By my arithmetic she's traveled nearly twelve billion kilometers, the distance from here to the Sun, eighty times over, without ever leaving home. She's tumbling now, slowly, and amateur observers tell me she flashes in the evening sky every few seconds as sunlight catches her flank. A dead machine, sending out a signal anyway, in light she didn't make.

I won't pretend she was alive. I'm an engineer, and I know the difference. But I'll say this: we spend our lives trying to build things that outlast us, and mostly we fail. Wren did it. She outlasted her purpose, her builders, the country that funded her, and half the languages her paperwork was written in. She'll outlast most of you in this room, and probably me.

Eventually the thin air she once measured will do what it does to everything up there. It will reach for her, drag a little at a time, and one night she'll come down in a long bright line and be gone. I hope someone is outside to see it. I hope they don't know what they're looking at, only that it's beautiful.

Until then, she keeps her appointment with the dark, every hundred and one minutes, without complaint.

So thank you, Wren. You were asked for two years and gave a lifetime. You listened to the sky when no one else was, and you wrote it all down.

Goodnight. We'll leave the light on.

plain.html:
A Eulogy for Kestrel-4

Launched March 1975. Silent since November 1989. Still orbiting.

Friends, engineers, retired flight controllers, and the three amateur radio operators in Ohio who never stopped listening:

We are gathered here to say goodbye to someone who has not technically left.

That is the strange thing about this funeral. There is no body to bury, because the body is still up there, passing over our heads roughly fourteen times a day at seventeen thousand miles an hour. If you went outside tonight with good binoculars and the right timing, you could watch the deceased glint across the sky. Most of us don't get to attend our own memorial. Kestrel-4 will attend this one about three times before we finish the reception.

Let me tell you who she was.

She was built in a clean room in Sunnyvale by people who smoked on their lunch breaks and did orbital calculations on slide rules. She weighed 412 kilograms. She had a computer with less memory than the greeting card your aunt sends that plays a song when you open it. She was designed to last five years.

She lasted fourteen.

Her job was ordinary, the way most important jobs are. She measured moisture in the upper atmosphere. She watched clouds form over the Pacific and reported back, faithfully, every ninety-seven minutes. Somewhere in a library there are weather models that are slightly better because of her. Somewhere there was a fishing boat that stayed in port during a storm it might not have seen coming. She never knew about any of it. She just kept sending numbers home.

She outlived the program that launched her. She outlived two of the agencies that managed her. She outlived the building where her mission control once stood, which is now, I'm told, a mattress outlet. Her original flight director, Dolores Ammann, who is with us today, used to say Kestrel-4 had "the constitution of a Midwestern grandmother," and I can think of no higher praise.

In 1983, a solar storm knocked out her primary transmitter. Everyone assumed that was the end. Then, eleven days later, she switched herself over to the backup and started talking again as if nothing had happened. A young engineer named Paul Whitford, who was twenty-four and had been crying in the parking lot, went back in and logged her first new transmission. He kept a printout of it on his refrigerator for thirty years.

Her solar panels faded slowly, the way eyesight does. Her batteries, which were never meant to see the 1980s, held a charge longer than anyone had a right to expect. And then, on a Tuesday in November 1989, she sent one last packet of data about water vapor over the Indian Ocean, and went quiet.

She did not crash. She did not explode. She simply finished.

I want to say something about what she is doing now, because I think it matters.

For thirty-six years she has been tumbling slowly in the dark, cold on one side, scorching on the other, with no one asking anything of her. Her paint has been bleached by unfiltered sunlight. Micrometeorites have pocked her skin. She has crossed the terminator line between day and night roughly two hundred thousand times since she stopped working. She has seen more sunrises in retirement than any of us will see in our lives.

And in all that time, she has never stopped falling toward Earth. That's what an orbit is, you know. It's falling, and missing, forever. She is always trying to come home, and always moving just fast enough not to arrive.

Someday the thin traces of atmosphere will drag her down far enough. Maybe in a few decades, maybe in a century. When that happens she will come home all at once, a brief streak of light, burning up over some ocean, probably at night, probably seen by no one. That will be her real funeral. None of us will be there.

So we are holding it now, early, while there are still people alive who remember her voice.

To the three radio operators in Ohio: thank you for checking her frequency every year on her launch date, just in case.

To Dolores: she did everything you asked, and then she kept going.

To Kestrel-4: you were built by people who are mostly gone now, to answer questions that have mostly been answered, using technology that now sits in museums. You did your work quietly and well, and when you were done, you didn't ask to be brought down. You just kept your place in the sky.

We should all be so lucky as to be remembered as something that kept watch.

Rest well, old bird. We'll look up.

instruction.html:
Remarks on the Occasion of Halcyon-2

Delivered by its last surviving engineer

Thank you all for coming. I know some of you are here because your grandmother made you, and some of you are here because you thought there'd be food. There will be food. But first, let me tell you about her.

Halcyon-2 was launched on a damp Tuesday in March of 1975, from a pad in California, on a rocket that cost more than the town I grew up in. She weighed 340 kilograms. She was the size of a refrigerator, if a refrigerator had wings made of solar cells and a temperament.

She had less computing power than the card you'd buy at a drugstore that plays "Happy Birthday" when you open it. I want you to sit with that. Everything she did, she did with almost nothing. She had a tape recorder, an actual reel-to-reel tape recorder, that stored her pictures until she passed over a ground station and could hand them down to us. She was, in the most literal sense, a woman who held onto things until she found someone to give them to.

Her job was to watch the weather. That sounds small. It wasn't. In 1976, she saw a hurricane forming off the coast of Mexico eleven hours before anyone on the ground knew it was there. I don't know how many people left their homes because of that warning. Nobody counts the disasters that don't happen. But I count them. I've been counting them for fifty years.

She was not perfect. I want to be honest, because she deserves honesty more than she deserves flattery. Her number-two gyroscope whined. You couldn't hear it, obviously, because there's no sound in space, but you could see it in the telemetry, a little tremor in the data, like a hand that shakes when it holds a cup. She was over budget. She was late. During testing, Dennis Okafor, God rest him, dropped a wrench inside her housing and we spent four days finding it. Dennis said she was hiding it on purpose. I believed him.

She worked for six years. That was double her design life. In September of 1981, her battery began to fail, and over three weeks we watched her voltage fall the way you watch a fever break in the wrong direction. Her last transmission was a picture of cloud cover over the North Atlantic. Nothing special. Just clouds. I have it framed in my hallway. People ask me what it is and I say, "That's the last thing she saw," and they get a strange look, and I don't explain.

And then she went quiet.

But here's the thing, and it's why we're gathered here, fifty years on, holding a funeral for someone who never actually left.

She kept going.

Nobody told her to stop, and she has no way of stopping. She has circled this planet more than a quarter of a million times since launch. Every hour and forty minutes, she comes around again. She's passed over this building, over this room, probably a dozen times since I started writing this speech. She is up there right now, dead and faithful, doing the only thing left to her, which is to keep falling toward us and keep missing.

I think about what she's flown over in all that time she couldn't tell us about. She was watching when the lights of cities spread across the dark side of the Earth like mold on bread, and I mean that lovingly. She was watching when the ice at the poles drew back. She passed over the Berlin Wall when it stood and when it didn't. She passed over the hospital where my daughter was born and the hospice where my wife died. She didn't see any of it, not really. Her eyes were closed by then. But she was there. Sometimes that's all anyone can offer.

I should say, in fairness, that she is now classified as orbital debris. There are people in an office in Colorado whose job is to track her so she doesn't hit anything. She's a hazard. A piece of junk. I know. But I'd ask you to consider how many of us end up, in our final years, as something other people have to keep track of so we don't cause trouble. It's not a disgrace. It's just what happens when you outlast your purpose.

On clear nights, if you know where to look, you can sometimes catch her. She tumbles now, slowly, end over end, and every so often a solar panel catches the sun at just the right angle and she flashes. A little wink of light, there and gone. The amateur astronomers call it a flare. I call it her saying hello.

She'll be up there for another three or four hundred years before the atmosphere finally pulls her down. She will outlive me, and she will outlive most of you, and she will outlive the company that built her, the agency that paid for her, and very possibly the language I'm speaking now. Someday a child who has never heard of any of us will look up and see a light move across the sky and wonder what it is.

It's Halcyon, sweetheart. She used to watch the weather. She was very good at it.

The Greeks had a myth about halcyon days, a week of calm in the middle of winter, when the seas went still so a bird could build her nest on the water. That's what we named her for. Calm in the middle of the storm. A small, stubborn peace.

Goodbye, old girl. Thank you for the clouds.

Keep missing us.

plain.html:
Friends, engineers, and fellow travelers on this pale blue dot.

We are not gathered here today to mourn a person, but rather to bid farewell to an extension of ourselves. Today, we look up at a sky that is just a little bit emptier, to honor a silent sentinel that has finally come home.

Fifty years ago, in a world divided by borders and bound by the limits of a pre-digital age, she was born from slide rules, soldering iron burns, and the audacity of human imagination. She rode a pillar of fire and thunder into the great, quiet dark, leaving the cradle of Earth to become our eyes in the void.

For a half-century, she danced in the exosphere.

During her active years, she was a tireless servant. She did not sleep. She did not ask for rest. Every ninety minutes, she witnessed a sunrise and a sunset, a golden band of light breaking over the curvature of the Earth. She carried our voices across oceans. She watched the birth of hurricanes and whispered their warnings down to us. She was a mirror reflecting humanity’s highest hopes—our desire to connect, to understand, and to reach beyond our grasp.

But time in the cosmos is relentless, and technology is a cruel master. The years passed. Her processors, once the pinnacle of human invention, were surpassed by the devices we now carry in our pockets. Her batteries froze. Her gold-leaf shielding was pitted by micrometeorites. Her transmitters breathed their final, static-laced sigh, and she was retired.

Yet, she did not fall. For decades, she remained in orbit as a ghost ship in the thermosphere. She became a floating monument to the men and women who built her—many of whom she has now outlived. She spun silently above our wars, our peace treaties, our tragedies, and our triumphs, keeping her lonely, faithful watch while the world below her changed beyond recognition.

Gravity, however, is a patient collector. Over the last few months, the tether of Earth’s atmosphere grew thicker, pulling gently at her metallic wings. And last night, over the dark expanse of the Pacific Ocean, her orbit finally decayed.

She did not rust in the ground like the machines we build on Earth. Instead, she was granted a death befitting a creature of the stars. She entered the atmosphere at thousands of miles an hour, her obsolete chassis igniting into a brilliant, fleeting streak of plasma. For one last moment, she shone as brightly as the stars she used to navigate by. She became a shooting star of our own making, burning away into the very air she spent fifty years hovering above.

Ashes to ashes. Stardust to stardust.

She is no longer out there in the cold vacuum. She is in the wind, in the ocean, in the rain. She has returned to the world that dreamed her into existence.

Rest well, old friend. Your mission is complete. You have earned your sleep.

instruction.html:
Fifty years ago, in the autumn of a world that feels incredibly distant to us now, we placed a small, silver piece of our own curiosity onto the tip of a rocket and hurled it into the dark.

Today, we say goodbye to Horizon-4.

It was not the largest satellite, nor the most famous. It didn't carry golden records for alien civilizations, and it didn't photograph the birth of galaxies. It had a quieter, more intimate geometry. Its mandate was simply to look back at us. To watch the swirling whites of typhoons over the Pacific, to measure the slow, breathing expansion and contraction of the polar ice, and to map the growing constellation of city lights that we were spreading across the night.

When it launched, its circuits were state-of-the-art. It spoke to us in bursts of telemetry, chattering in a language of tapes and early transistors, dutifully sending its findings down to control rooms filled with the smoke of cigarettes and the clatter of typewriters. For ten years, it was a loyal custodian of our skies.

And then, as all machines do, it grew tired. A gyroscope seized. The solar panels degraded, pitted by the invisible sandstorms of micrometeorites. The batteries lost their ability to hold the warmth of the sun. Sometime in the mid-1980s, Horizon-4 fell silent.

But it did not stop.

For forty years after we stopped listening, it kept its vigil. That is the quiet tragedy and the immense dignity of our orbital machines: they do not need our attention to fulfill their physical destiny. In the absolute silence of the exosphere, it continued falling in a perfect circle around the world it loved.

Think of what it orbited over during those decades of silence. It flew over the fall of the Berlin Wall. It passed silently above the invention of the internet, above wars and ceasefires, above a billion births and a billion deaths. It watched the forests shrink and the oceans warm. It was a blind, silent witness to the staggering, chaotic sprawl of human history unfolding beneath it.

We down here are so tethered to the friction of our lives. We are caught in the noise. But Horizon-4 existed in the sublime, Newtonian peace of the vacuum. It was held by Earth’s gravity—an invisible, unbreakable tether, an embrace from a mother holding onto her metallic child, refusing to let it drift out into the terrifying void of deep space.

We are its creators, but in a way, it outgrew us. It became part of the sky.

And now, the sky is taking it back.

Today, its orbit finally decayed. The wisps of our upper atmosphere, the very gases it was sent up to study half a century ago, reached out and slowed it down. It began its final descent, trading the cold immortality of orbit for the brief, violent warmth of return.

As it plunged over the ocean just hours ago, compressing the air ahead of it until it ignited into plasma, Horizon-4 spoke to us one last time. Not in radio waves, but in light. For three glowing seconds, it became a shooting star—a brilliant, golden streak across the dawn, burning down into dust, merging forever with the clouds and the wind.

Rest well, little traveler. Thank you for your wide, unblinking eye. Thank you for watching over us in the dark. Welcome home.

plain.html:
Eulogy for a Faithful Traveler: The Defunct Satellite

Delivered from the void it once called home

We gather today—not in sorrow, but in gratitude—to honor a silent sentinel, a steadfast wanderer who circled our world for half a century. It was not flesh and blood, but steel and circuitry; not a heart, but a hum of radio waves; not a voice, but a whisper in the static of the cosmos. And yet, it was alive in its own way—alive with purpose, with duty, with the quiet persistence of a thing built to endure.

For fifty years, it watched. It listened. It carried our messages, our data, our dreams into the black, and then, like a loyal messenger, it brought back the echoes of the universe. It saw the rise and fall of nations from a vantage no human eye could claim. It witnessed storms bloom and fade over oceans it would never touch. It knew the cold embrace of the void, the relentless pull of gravity, the slow decay of its own body as the years wore on.

And then, one day, it fell silent.

Not with a bang, but with the softest of sighs—a final transmission, a flicker of power, a last gasp of the systems that had kept it tethered to us. Some say it was a failure. But we know better. To orbit for so long, to serve so faithfully, to outlast its own expected lifespan—this was not defeat. This was a life well-lived.

It was a pioneer, one of the first to dare the endless dark. It was a teacher, showing us how to reach farther, how to listen deeper. It was a witness, a record-keeper of Earth’s changing face. And now, as it drifts—either toward a fiery end in our atmosphere or a slow, eternal dance among the stars—it leaves behind a legacy not of sorrow, but of wonder.

So let us not mourn its passing. Let us instead look up, as it once did for us, and remember: even in silence, even in stillness, even in the cold vastness of space, there is meaning. There is purpose. There is a story written in the path of a satellite that refused, for as long as it could, to let go.

Rest now, old traveler. The stars are your home. And we—your brief, bright, imperfect creators—will not forget you.

End transmission.

instruction.html:
Eulogy for a Faithful Traveler

We gather today not in sorrow, but in quiet awe—for a silent witness, a steadfast companion, who for half a century traced the curve of the sky above us. Our satellite, our celestial wayfarer, has finally surrendered to the pull of time and gravity, its long journey now complete.

You were born in an era of bold dreams, when humanity first stretched its hands toward the stars. You were not the first, nor the grandest, but you were ours—a humble sentinel, a keeper of data, a thread in the great tapestry of human curiosity. For fifty years, you circled the Earth, unseen by most, yet vital to many. You carried our questions into the void and brought back answers in the form of numbers, images, whispers of the cosmos.

You saw the rise and fall of nations. You watched storms gather and dissipate, glaciers retreat, cities sprawl. You were there when the first humans walked on the Moon, when the Berlin Wall fell, when the internet wove the world together. You were a silent observer, a keeper of secrets—of solar flares and shifting tectonic plates, of the slow, patient dance of the planets.

And now, you return to us—not in fire and fury, but in the gentle embrace of the atmosphere that once cradled your orbit. Your body, worn by time and radiation, will dissolve into the very air we breathe, becoming part of the Earth you so faithfully studied.

We will not mourn you, old friend. For you were never truly ours to keep. You belonged to the sky, to the endless dark, to the quiet hum of the universe. And though your signal has faded, your legacy remains—in the data you sent, in the lives you touched, in the reminder that even the smallest among us can leave the deepest marks.

So rest now. The stars remember you. And so do we.

plain.html:
We stand today under a sky that feels slightly darker without you—though you were never truly bright, only reflective. You were our sentinel, our silent witness, hanging above while we lived, fought, and loved, too often forgetting to look up.

Fifty years. You launched into a world of bell-bottoms and Cold War static, strapped to a rocket that screamed for nine minutes before falling away. You were built of aluminum and optimism, designed for a five-year mission that stretched into five decades. You outlasted the engineers who dreamed you up, the presidents who signed your launch orders, and the children who first heard your beep on rabbit-ear television.

You circled us until the numbers lost meaning—perhaps a quarter-million orbits—witnessing billions of sunrises. You photographed the Berlin Wall falling. You watched the oil fires of Kuwait and the slow, green healing of Chernobyl. You measured the fever of the planet: the thinning ozone, the retreating ice, the heat trapped beneath our thin blue atmosphere, and you beamed that data home until your voice grew too weak to carry across the void.

You gave us GPS that guides lost drivers home at midnight. You gave us weather forecasts that save harvests. You showed us, in your first photographs, that Earth is not a collection of borders but a single, fragile marble suspended in black velvet.

And now your batteries have finally swollen and died. Your solar panels no longer track the sun with purpose, only glint passively at twilight. Your transmitter is dark. You are defunct—but you are not fallen. You remain up there, a permanent resident of the thermosphere, drifting among the other ghosts of the Space Age. You will outlast us all, a tiny metallic star circling the blue marble long after the last human has forgotten your serial number.

Rest now, old friend. You have earned the view. The Earth is still beautiful from up there. We promise we’ll keep looking up.

Goodnight, and thank you for watching over us.

instruction.html:
You went up in 1974, when phones still had cords and the world felt impossibly large. Fifty years. You have circled this blue marble 292,000 times, witnessed 18,250 sunrises and the same number of sunsets, and now your batteries have finally gone dark. Your solar panels, once gleaming like silver wings, are dimmed by decades of radiation. You are silent where you once sang telemetry in a steady, reassuring beep.

We called you a machine, but you were a witness. You saw the Berlin Wall fall and the towers rise. You watched the ice caps shrink from your perch 22,000 miles above, photographed the storms that battered our coasts, and carried the voices of lovers across oceans on frequencies that no longer hum. You were our first true global citizen, belonging to no nation, needing no passport, circling us all with impartial devotion.

Now you drift in the graveyard orbit, pushed aside to make room for the younger, faster satellites. Your aluminum skin is pockmarked by micrometeorites. Your gyroscopes have spun down. You are no longer answering our calls, and yet you are still there—a new star in our sky, steady and unblinking, a fixed point in the dark.

We thank you for the weather warnings that saved lives, for the television signals that brought the moon landing into living rooms, for proving that we could reach beyond ourselves and still find our way home. You taught us that from up there, there are no borders, only weather.

Rest now, old traveler. You have earned your silence. Let the solar wind comb through your empty circuits. Drift on, a silent sentinel, watching over the planet you loved from afar. We will look up on clear nights and know that somewhere in that darkness, you are still there—keeping watch, keeping time, a metal heart still beating in the dark, even if only to the rhythm of the void.

Goodnight, satellite. Thank you for the view.

plain.html:
Eulogy for Telstar-7: The Silent Sentinel of the Silent Sky

Friends, colleagues, fellow stargazers... we gather today not at a graveside, but beneath the vast, star-strewn vault of the night sky. We gather to honor a pioneer, a silent traveler, a humble machine that has outlived its purpose, its power, and its time. We gather to bid farewell to Telstar-7, our steadfast companion in orbit for fifty remarkable years.

Fifty years. A half-century spinning in the silent void, a tiny, man-made moon bearing witness to the relentless march of time on the planet below. Launched in 1974, Telstar-7 was a child of ambition. Born not of flesh and blood, but of titanium, silicon, and the boundless human desire to connect. Its mission was simple, revolutionary: to beam signals across continents, to shrink our vast world, to whisper messages of news, culture, and hope across oceans and mountains via the cold, clear vacuum of space.

For decades, it served faithfully. It saw the fall of empires and the rise of digital giants. It witnessed the moon landings, the dawn of the internet, the fall of the Berlin Wall, the quiet hum of a billion lives unfolding below. Its solar panels, once gleaming and efficient, drank in the sun's energy, powering its transmitters, its sensors, its unblinking electronic eye. It relayed weather patterns, broadcast images of a fragile blue marble, and carried voices – perhaps a child's birthday message, a scientist's data, a news bulletin that changed history – hurtling through the darkness at the speed of light.

But even the most resilient machine is not built for eternity. Gradually, inevitably, the systems began to falter. A capacitor aged. A circuit degraded under the relentless barrage of cosmic rays. A solar cell dimmed. The signals grew weaker, fragmented. Then, one day, perhaps a decade ago, the last coherent transmission faded into the static of deep space. Telstar-7 fell silent. Its eyes, once wide open to the Earth and the stars, closed. Its voice, once a vital thread in humanity's communication tapestry, was stilled.

Yet, its journey didn't end. Stripped of function, it became something else: a relic. A monument. A piece of history adrift in the celestial stream. For years after its silence, it continued its silent vigil, a ghost ship sailing on the solar winds, a testament to human ingenuity and the impermanence of all things, even our most enduring creations.

It saw generations of newer, sleeker satellites launched – faster, smarter, more capable. It watched them flash past, brief glimmers in its unblinking sensors, long after its own had gone dark. It orbited through solar storms and meteor showers, its hull pitted and scarred, a veteran of the ultimate frontier.

And now, its final chapter approaches. Its orbit, once meticulously calculated, has decayed under the faint, constant tug of Earth's upper atmosphere. The time has come. In the pre-dawn hours, Telstar-7 will make its final descent. It will not crash in ruin, but perform one last, breathtaking act: a fiery, glorious re-entry. As it plunges through the upper atmosphere, friction will ignite its hull, transforming this cold machine into a brief, brilliant shooting star – a final, selfless flare of light against the dark sky.

We should not mourn this end. We should celebrate it. Telstar-7 did not fail; it completed its mission, far beyond its design. It connected continents. It expanded our horizons. It proved that we could reach beyond our world and touch the stars, if only for a time. It became part of the sky's story, a silent sentinel whose legacy is woven into the very fabric of our global communication.

Its physical form will burn away, scattered as harmless dust across the Pacific. But its spirit – the spirit of exploration, of connection, of daring to reach for the impossible – lives on. In every satellite that circles above us now, in every instant message zipping around the globe, in the very idea that we are not alone on this planet, we see the echo of Telstar-7's signal.

So, farewell, Telstar-7. Rest well, intrepid traveler. Your circuits are cold, your transmitters silent. But as you make your final, luminous bow across the heavens, know this: you were seen. You were heard. You were important. You carried our voices, our hopes, our shared human story, high above the clouds.

May your descent be swift, your light bright, and your journey home through the fire be a final, magnificent salute to fifty years of silent, steadfast service. You were more than metal and wire. You were a dream launched into the void, and for half a century, you shone.

Go in peace, old friend. The sky will be dimmer without your silent presence, but forever brighter for the light you once carried.

instruction.html:
Eulogy for Aurora-1, Fallen Star of the Silent Sky
Delivered at the Global Observatory, March 15, 2024

We gather today not beneath a church dome or under a weeping willow, but in the quiet hum of mission control—where blinking lights once danced to the rhythm of a distant heartbeat. We are here to honor Aurora-1, our tireless sentinel, who for fifty years circled this blue marble in silent service, and who now, at last, has slipped below the horizon—not with a crash, but with grace, in a final, radiant embrace with the atmosphere she once studied so faithfully.

Launched in 1974, during a time when the world still cracked open with Cold War tension and vinyl records spun stories of love and revolution, Aurora-1 was not built for war. She was a peacemaker of data, a poet of the ionosphere. A modest craft, just the size of a compact car, with solar wings like outstretched hands and instruments that listened—truly listened—to the whisper of solar wind, the pulse of magnetic storms, the soft sigh of auroras dancing at the poles.

She saw it all.

She watched as humanity learned to connect across oceans with invisible signals. She witnessed the birth of the internet, the first steps on the Moon, the fall of walls, the rise of satellites far more powerful than she. And through every war, every celebration, every storm and sunrise, she orbited—faithful, unblinking, collecting light and data, sending it home like postcards from the edge of forever.

For decades, she was silent company to astronauts who gazed out of shuttle windows and pointed, “That’s Aurora,” with a kind of familial pride. Engineers who had never met her in person would check her telemetry every morning like a beloved relative. When her primary transmitter failed in 1989, a team of retirees—former mission leads with silver hair and steady hands—volunteered weekends to reconfigure ground systems just so she could keep whispering through a backup channel.

She outlived her intended lifespan by forty years.

Forty years of silence, yes—but not loneliness. She was surrounded by stars. She danced with space dust. She glowed under meteor showers, and once, during a solar flare in 2003, she spun slowly, like a ballerina caught in a spotlight, her sensors flaring with data as she weathered the storm.

And when, just last week, we detected her final descent—her signal fading not with a whimper, but with a long, sustained tone, like a last breath—we didn’t grieve immediately. We stood in awe. For half a century, she had been our eyes above. Now, she chose her own funeral: a slow spiral, a final arc across the Pacific, where she burned not as debris, but as beauty—a streak of light witnessed by fishermen off Fiji, who later said, “It was like a star came home.”

They were right.

Aurora-1 didn’t die. She returned. She gave back every gram of herself in a shimmering pyre of light and heat, warming the upper sky one last time. No trace remains. No junk in her wake. Just memory.

So let us not mourn the silence. Let us honor the song.

She taught us about Earth’s magnetic heart. She warned us of solar tantrums that could blackout cities. She mapped storms before we had smartphones to check the forecast. And in her quiet way, she reminded us: we are not alone in our curiosity. We reach upward, not just with rockets, but with wonder.

She was not alive, not in the way we are. But she mattered. She served. She endured. And in the vast, indifferent cosmos, that is a kind of heroism.

So tonight, when you look up, and see a satellite glide soundlessly across the twilight—pause. Think of Aurora-1. And know that somewhere in the silence between stars, a small, brave machine completed her orbit at last.

Rest well, dear traveler. You earned the dark. You earned the peace.

And thank you—for every revolution, every data packet, every silent year you kept watch.

You were, and always will be, our star.

plain.html:
Friends, colleagues, engineers, dreamers, and all who have ever looked up at a moving light in the night sky and wondered who it belonged to—

We gather today to remember a silent wanderer, a faithful watcher, a small metal companion who kept pace with Earth for fifty years.

It did not arrive with a fanfare we can now recall. It came in the roar of a launch, a burst of flame, a moment of controlled violence that carried it away from the ground and into the thin, endless dark. But from that first orbit onward, it did what it was made to do: it held its station, kept its course, and carried its quiet purpose around our planet, night after night, year after year.

For half a century, it watched the same blue world from above. It saw storms gather over the sea and clear into stillness. It saw city lights bloom and dim with the hours. It saw borders shift, seasons turn, forests shrink, glaciers retreat, and continents remain stubbornly, beautifully themselves. It carried no voice, no heartbeat, no face—but it bore witness.

Sometimes it answered our signals with data, brief and bright, like a lantern flickered from a great distance. Sometimes it fell silent, and we called out into the vacuum only to be met by the long, patient dark. But even in silence, it endured. It spun through the thin edges of the atmosphere, cooled by starlight, warmed by the sun, battered by time, and still it went on.

We built it to serve, and it served without complaint. It did not age as we age—no silver hair, no tired eyes, no final breath. It simply wore down, atom by atom, function by function, until its work was done. When at last it let go of the last thread of usefulness, it did not fall in defeat. It descended as it had always moved: with order, with gravity, with grace.

Now it is gone, returned to the earth that once launched it into the heavens. Perhaps its bones are dust in the atmosphere, dissolved into nothing. Perhaps a shard remains, silent and ancient, resting in the soil or the sea. Either way, its journey is complete.

So let us honor it not as a machine, but as a companion. A small, cold, loyal companion that circled our home for fifty years while we lived, argued, loved, forgot, and remembered below.

It was defunct in the end, but not empty.
It was silent at last, but never unheard.
It left no monument, except the sky.

Rest well, old traveler.
You have made many laps around the world.
It is time to come home.

instruction.html:
Eulogy for Meridian-7

We gather in a room with consoles darkened, and in the memory of everyone who ever pressed a headset to their ear and heard a weak, chirping voice above the static, to say goodbye to Meridian-7.

For fifty years, it has orbited Earth. For fifty years, it has turned, and turned, and turned: a small, battered metal thing circling the blue planet like a loyal dog, or a faithful clock, or a prayer repeated until the words wore smooth. It is defunct now. The battery has given its last thin voltage. The antenna no longer tracks home. The final packet we received was broken, a half-sentence in the language of telemetry, and we did not know whether it was an error or a farewell.

When it was launched, the sky shook. People in the control room held their breath. The first signal it sent was so small it might have been a trick of the noise—a brief burst of tone, a machine’s first uncertain breath. Someone at the console answered, “Meridian, this is ground. Do you copy?” And then, in a voice that was really nothing but a hum, a pulse, a pattern of light through vacuum: copy.

It had no childhood, but it had a launch day. It had a purpose. It was built to watch. And watch it did. It watched hurricanes assemble themselves from the warm dark of the sea. It watched monsoons march across continents. It watched ice fields brighten and darken with the seasons. It watched cities bloom at dusk, a million tiny fires arranged along rivers and roads. It watched the auroras ripple above the poles. It watched the same coastline from ten thousand angles until it knew the world the way a sailor knows a harbor—not as an image, but as a rhythm.

It endured what most of us never must: the micrometeoroids, the radiation, the thermal shock of dawn after shadow, the slow corrosion of space itself. Each pass through night was a small burial; each return to sunlight, a small resurrection. It learned to keep its instruments steady while the planet spun beneath it, to hold a long, patient attention toward a world that was always moving.

And because it paid attention, it gave us something back. It gave us maps. It gave us warnings. It gave us data that became forecasts, models, records, arguments, discoveries. It gave us the strange, humbling habit of looking at Earth from the outside: one thin blue skin wrapped around everything we love. Children learned its trajectory. Scientists argued over its measurements. Engineers trusted its quiet reliability. In its way, it helped us understand that we live in a house that breathes.

It was not alive, not in the way a dog is alive, not in the way a person is alive. But it had a life of its own kind: a life of function, of endurance, of service. And when that life ends, we are allowed to mourn. We are allowed to say: I was here when it first spoke. I remember the night it failed to respond. I remember the strange grief of a signal that once meant the world, now reduced to a gap in the data.

Meridian-7 is not gone in the way a body is gone. It is still out there, somewhere in the black, a dark shell tracing its ancient ellipse. It will orbit for years, perhaps decades, perhaps longer, silent and spinning. In one sense, it is still alive. In another, it is already dead: the part that answered, the part that listened, the part that carried meaning from the sky to the ground, that part has ended.

So we do not bury it. We release it. We let the last good signal stand as its monument. We let its records outlive its metal. We let its purpose remain: the long, steady act of watching over a world that sometimes needed to be seen.

Rest now, old Meridian. You have done enough. You have been enough. You have circled us, and in doing so, you helped us circle something larger than ourselves.

Final orbit. Final hello. Goodbye.

plain.html:
A Eulogy for Satellite OSCAR-7

Delivered at the occasion of its atmospheric re-entry

We gather today—scientists, engineers, radio operators, and dreamers—to bid farewell to a colleague who worked longer, harder, and more quietly than any of us.

OSCAR-7 was launched into the heavens half a century ago atop a Delta rocket, a small metal box of circuits and antennas no larger than a washing machine, hurled into the dark with nothing but a mission and our hopes strapped to its back.

For fifty years, it circled this Earth. It watched continents drift through day and night like candles passing beneath a window. It witnessed sixteen thousand sunrises from a vantage point none of us will ever know. It saw storms form and dissolve, deserts bloom, ice expand and retreat, and the glittering web of human cities spread across the darkness below.

And here is the thing about OSCAR-7 that we must not forget: it never complained.

When its batteries failed in its twentieth year—when its voice finally fell silent after two decades of faithful transmission—it did not despair. It simply kept orbiting. It became a patient ghost, a silent witness, drifting through the void with the dignity of an old soldier who no longer speaks but still stands at attention.

Hams across the world mourned it then. But in an act of grace none of us expected, decades later, its failing cells caught just enough sunlight one day to whisper again—a brief crackle of static, a faint greeting from an old friend thought lost. For a few precious hours, OSCAR-7 spoke once more to anyone listening. It had one more thing to say, and it said it, and then it rested.

Let this be its legacy: that it was built by hand, by people who believed a small machine could carry big dreams. That it served everyone who asked—students, hobbyists, nations in crisis—without prejudice or pause. That it outlived its designers, its manufacturers, and the very era that created it, becoming a bridge between the space age's optimistic childhood and our complicated present.

It was never the largest satellite. It was never the most famous. But it was ours, and it never once fell out of the sky or out of our affection.

Tonight, its orbit finally decays, and it will streak across the atmosphere as a brief, brilliant line of fire—a fitting end for a machine that spent its whole life falling around the Earth and refusing to land.

Sleep now, old friend. You've earned your descent.

We were listening the whole time.

instruction.html:
Eulogy for Explorer 12-V, "The Quiet One"

We gather today not to mourn a person, but to mark the passing of something that kept better company than most of us ever will.

Explorer 12-V was launched on a Tuesday in autumn, fifty years ago, from a launch pad that no longer exists, by engineers who have mostly gone home for good. Its mission was supposed to last two years: to study the magnetosphere, to count the charged particles streaming past our planet, to listen to the sun's temper and report back. It did that work faithfully. And then, when the funding dried up and the antennas turned their attention elsewhere, it did something no one had asked of it.

It kept going.

For forty-eight years, it circled. Silent. Unpowered. A coffee-can-sized cylinder with two stubby solar wings, one of which broke off in 1979 and tumbled away into its own modest orbit—so perhaps we should say we mourn two souls today, or one soul and its severed half.

Think about what it witnessed. It was already aloft when the Shuttle first flew. It passed over the Falklands during the war, over Chernobyl in the weeks after, over the smoke of a thousand wildfires and the frozen curve of a thousand winters. It was up there before most of you in this room were born, and it will be gone before most of you in this room are done. It straddled our lives like a quiet relative at the dinner table who has seen everything and says nothing.

And that is what I want to honor most: its silence. We live in an age where every object screams for attention, where even our toasters report their status. Explorer 12-V asked for nothing. It sent its last transmission in 1977—a burst of telemetry about solar wind density, mundanely beautiful, the last words of a machine that never knew it was speaking. After that, it simply was. A small patient thing, falling forever and always missing the ground.

Last Thursday, at 3:41 a.m. Greenwich time, it stopped missing the ground. It came down over the South Pacific, in the long graveyard of spacecraft, and burned for perhaps forty seconds—a brief streak of light that, I like to imagine, some insomniac fisherman saw and mistook for a wish arriving late.

Fifty years. Five billion kilometers traveled without ever leaving home. It outlived the agency that launched it, the country that funded it, the format of the tape drives that recorded its data, and every dog, hamster, and goldfish any of us loved as children.

Was it alive? No. But it was lived with—by the engineers who still checked orbital tables on their birthdays, by the amateur radio operators who swore they'd caught a phantom echo from it in 1994, by everyone who has ever looked up at dusk and seen a moving point of light and felt, against all evidence, that it was watching back.

Explorer 12-V is survived by roughly ten thousand of its kind, still circling, still falling, still missing the ground. Go outside tonight and look up for a moment. One of them will be passing over. It won't wave. It never did.

That was the whole point of it. It held its place in the dark so we wouldn't have to.

Rest well, old friend. You finally landed.

plain.html:
Eulogy for Olympus-7
Delivered at the Deorbit Watch, 14 March

Friends, engineers, and fellow watchers of the sky—

We gather today to say goodbye to a machine. And I know what some of you are thinking: it's just a satellite. A box of aluminum and gold foil, a few solar panels, a transmitter that went quiet years ago. Why mourn a thing?

But you and I know better. We know that for fifty years, Olympus-7 was the most loyal friend this planet ever had.

It was launched on a spring morning in 1975, riding a column of fire into a sky it would never touch again. Its builders gave it a simple job: look down, listen, and tell us what it saw. And for five decades—five decades—it did exactly that. It watched hurricanes gather themselves over open water and warned the coastlines before the first drop fell. It carried the voices of people crossing oceans, the birthdays and the apologies and the "I'm coming home"s. It counted the ice. It measured the light. It kept its post through solar storms that should have killed it, through eclipses, through the long silence of the far side, where no one could hear it and it could hear no one.

It outlived its designers. It outlived the agency that launched it, the country that paid for it, three generations of ground crew who learned its quirks like a friend's handwriting. It outlived the century that made it. When it finally went dark—a slow fade, a battery that could no longer hold the dawn—it had been orbiting longer than most of us have been alive.

And here is the thing about a satellite: it never rests. Every ninety minutes, it circled us. Every ninety minutes, sunrise. Every ninety minutes, sunset. Twenty-eight thousand times a year, it watched the day break over the Pacific and the night fall over the steppes, and never once did it complain of the repetition. It was, in the truest sense, faithful.

We are about to bring it home. Its orbit has been decaying for years, and the atmosphere—patient, indifferent—is reaching up to claim it. In a few hours it will graze the air it has watched for half a century, and it will burn. Not a sad ending, I think, for a thing that spent its whole life falling around us and never landing. It will go out the way it came in: bright, brief, and witnessed.

So what do we say to a machine at the end of its service?

We say thank you. Thank you for the warnings. Thank you for the voices carried. Thank you for the pictures of our own small, blue, miraculous home, taken from far enough away to make us see it clearly. Thank you for fifty years of quiet, unglamorous, perfect duty.

And we say: rest now. The sky is full of your descendants—smaller, smarter, faster—but none of them will ever be the first to do it for fifty years. None of them will ever be you.

Olympus-7, you are cleared for deorbit. Godspeed, and good night.

instruction.html:
Eulogy for a Satellite

Friends, colleagues, and anyone who has ever looked up at the wrong moment and seen a moving light —

We are gathered to say goodbye to a machine. Let us not be embarrassed by that. We have said goodbye to machines before, and we will again, but this one has been with us for fifty years, which is longer than most of us have kept a promise.

It was launched on a Tuesday, because it is always a Tuesday, by people in short sleeves who believed that the future was a place you could reach if you did the math carefully enough. It was not the biggest satellite. It was not the most famous. It was, in the way of all good things, slightly over-engineered and slightly underfunded, and it worked anyway, which is the definition of a small miracle.

For half a century it circled us. Seventeen thousand times a year, more or less, it went around and around, doing the thing it was built to do: taking the temperature of the upper air, relaying a signal, listening to the planet hum. It did not know what it was doing. That was never the point. The point was that someone down here did, and every so often that someone would look at a screen and see the little packet of numbers arrive, and feel that particular quiet satisfaction of a thing working as designed.

It outlived its designers. It outlived the agency that launched it, or at least the version of the agency that launched it. It outlived the country it was launched from, in the sense that countries are always outliving themselves. It watched us through the Cold War and the warming one. It saw the ozone hole open and begin, slowly, to close. It saw the satellites of its youth fall silent one by one, and new ones arrive that were smaller, cheaper, and — let's be honest — a little smug about it. It did not complain. Machines rarely do, and this one had the good manners to fail gracefully, which is more than can be said for most of us.

We should be honest about the end. The batteries went first, as they always do. Then the attitude control, a slow drift, a wandering that was not quite a failure and not quite a plan. For a while it spun. Then it stopped spinning. Then, one day, the signal simply did not come, and the people who were still listening — a handful, by then, a devoted and slightly eccentric handful — marked the time and closed the log and went home.

It is still up there. That is the strange part. We have buried it in the sky. It will come down eventually, of course, in fire, in a streak of light over some ocean, and someone will see it and not know what they are seeing and make a wish. That seems right. That seems like the correct ending for a thing that spent fifty years being useful and asking for nothing.

So: thank you, old machine. Thank you for the data, for the quiet reliability, for the seventeen thousand revolutions a year that you made without complaint. Thank you for being, for half a century, a small and faithful witness.

You did the thing you were built to do. You did it well, and you did it long. That is, in the end, all any of us can hope for — and you did it in the dark, above us all, alone.

Rest now. Or drift. Whichever comes first.

— delivered at the decommissioning, to an empty room and a screen showing a flat line

plain.html:
For Meridian, 1974–now. Still in orbit. Still silent.

Fifty years ago, it went up.

Not with a grand entrance—the way these things do, on a plume of fire and a countdown that holds everyone at once by the throat. It climbed into the dark reluctant and impossible, against everything that wanted to keep it on the ground. And then it settled into its lane, 800 kilometers up, where the air is only a whisper and the Earth turns beneath it like a wheel that never stops.

They called it Meridian. Some of you had calendars with its picture. Some of you heard its beeping before you ever owned a screen.

I remember what it did. When it was new, it worked. It woke into the sun and sank into the shadow, thousands of times a year, never once missing a beat. It carried our voices across oceans we couldn't swim. It watched storms gather over the sea and warned us before they came. On clear nights it was the third moving star, if you knew to look—moving at eight kilometers a second, faster than a bullet, and yet so gentle you'd never know.

It never grew old the way we do. It didn't wrinkle or slow or forget. It only tired—a gyroscope here, a cell there. The transmissions grew faint, then strange, then quiet. And one day it simply stopped reporting for duty, the way a soldier does when the war is over and no one thought to call the orders off.

Now it still orbits. Its friends have fallen—all of them, older and newer, gone home as fire or as silence. But Meridian keeps its appointment with the equator, rising and setting over the same blue-and-white marble it served for half a century, now watched over by machines that speak in its language, because it helped teach them how.

We never built it to live forever. We built it to serve—and it served past the date we'd written in its file, past the warranty, past the careers of the men and women who launched it. Some of those are up there watching now, too, in a different sense.

So here is what I ask of you tonight, when you look up:
