When you see a faint light cross the dome of the sky—moving steady and unhurried, not blinking like an airplane, just passing—raise a glass, or a hand, or say nothing at all. That is enough. It asked for nothing while it was above us. It only gave.

And then let it go. Let it become what all our oldest servants eventually do: not a machine but a memory, not a signal but a silence we choose to remember as music.

Rest in orbit, little one. Your wheel is turned. The Earth is still here—still turning, still yours.

We saw you. We remembered. Thank you.

instruction.html:
We are gathered today to mark the passing of a quiet companion—one who never asked to come here, and who stayed far longer than anyone had a right to expect.

Fifty years ago, we sent it upward. Not with the grand ambitions we later handed our machines—no journeys to distant planets, no brave transmissions into the deep dark—but with something simpler. We wanted to reach. To leave the ground, and then to keep moving. It was our first restless thought, rendered in aluminum and glass and wired copper, singing its small signal back to a world that mostly didn't know to listen.

Think what it must have been like—to be so small and so high. To wake every ninety minutes into a sunrise it could do nothing but watch. To see the whole curve of a living planet roll beneath you, indifferent and beautiful, while everything you were built for happened far below, in the thin blue line where all our lives are spent.

It did its work, and then it did more. The mission ended; the orbit did not. Long after the last useful transmission, it kept circling—the faithful dog that never came inside, waiting at a door no one was watching. Engineers who trained for years to launch it lived out their lives on the ground while it simply went on, going on, a silver punctuation mark in a sentence with no end.

Consider what it saw from up there. Borders drawn and erased. Cities that were fields, and fields that became cities, and cities that glittered now where darkness had always been. Wars and weddings. Children born to people who would never know a single human being above the atmosphere had witnessed their smallest day—the flicker of a kitchen light at midnight, a boat crossing a black ocean, someone standing on a beach looking up and wondering if anything was looking back.

In a sense, it was. It looked back for us. It was our eye kept permanently open, our proof that we could send something out of ourselves into the cold and have it survive.

And here is the strange thing about saying goodbye to a thing like this: we know it was never alive. We know there was no one home inside the humming circuits, no longing in the solar panels turned toward a rising sun. And yet—after fifty years—it belongs to us now. It is part of the record of what we became. Long after the towers fall and the languages change and the name we gave it fades from every archive, it will still be up there, keeping its appointment with a planet that made it.

Eventually it will come home. That is the way of things that orbit—nothing rises without a debt to gravity, and everything that climbs is eventually invited back to earth. It will likely burn on the way down, giving itself back to the atmosphere in a single brief flash of light, brighter than any star, for less time than it takes to blink. Most of the world won't notice. A few people will look up and feel something they can't quite name.

That is the honor we give it today: to notice. To say that this small object, launched by hands now older, carried our curiosity and our hope through five decades of silent vigil, and asked for nothing in return but a little speed and a clear trajectory.

Thank you, old traveler. You reached. You kept moving. We saw you.

Rest now. The orbit is finished, and the ground has been patient all this time.

plain.html: It sounds like you’re caught between wanting to move on and still caring about them. That’s such a hard place to be. Do you think the attachment is more about loving them, or about the comfort of having them in your life?

instruction.html:
We are gathered here to honor a quiet pioneer. For fifty years, it has been a faithful sentinel in the sky, a silent witness to the changing world below.

It launched in 1974, a fragile construction of foil and circuitry, launched with the optimism of a new era. While we have forgotten the exact moment it began its long, lonely vigil, the people who watched it disappear into the horizon that day knew it well. They had built it, tested it, and talked to it. It had been their voice in the dark.

For decades, it transmitted signals to the rest of us — weather patterns, television broadcasts, the hum of a world becoming increasingly connected. We never saw it, but we relied on it. It became a mythos: always there, always watching, always speaking.

And now it is gone. Not because it failed, but because it simply ran out of time. Its circuits have finally tired, its signal has fallen silent, and it has slipped into the quiet of the thermosphere.

It leaves behind a legacy of connection. Every call made, every image received, every moment of shared experience was part of the world it helped build. It may have been just metal and code, but it carried our stories.

It has earned its rest. And we, who lived under its watchful eye, will remember it as the silent link that bound us together.

plain.html:
After fifty years of orbiting our planet, satellite 1234-2 has finally burned up in Earth’s atmosphere — a quiet, fiery end to a device that outlasted most of the technologies it was built to obsolete.

Launched in 1974 during the height of the Cold War, satellite 1234-2 spent decades circling the planet, bouncing signals from continent to continent, connecting military operations and covert missions across the globe. It was built to last five years in orbit. It survived nearly ten times longer — decades of radiation, micrometeoroid impacts, solar storms, and its own slow decay from atmospheric drag.

Over its lifetime, satellite 1234-2 witnessed the fall of empires, the rise of personal computing, the internet revolution, and the transformation of global communication into something almost unrecognizable from its own origins. It helped carry classified messages during proxy wars, guided rescue operations across oceans, and at some point — probably without anyone ever realizing — probably broadcast a stray TV signal or two into remote villages across the planet.

It didn’t get a funeral. No ceremony marked its retirement. Just a slow fade in telemetry data, a final confirmation from some ground station that it had gone silent. And now, its debris burns through the atmosphere at 1000°C for a few seconds — enough to make a pretty fireball if anyone had been looking up.

But somehow, that seems fitting. It served in silence. It died in silence. And now, its only legacy is a brief flash of light in the sky that nobody will notice — just like the thousands of other satellites that have come and gone since 1974.

Somewhere out there, however, there’s a retired engineer who built part of satellite 1234-2. They’ll feel something faint tonight. They’ll look up at the stars, not even sure which one was their satellite, but knowing somehow that one more piece of their life has finally found its ending.

instruction.html:
Orbiter 27

Satellite 0027 was launched on 14 May 1974 from the now-defunct Tyuratam Cosmodrome in what was then Soviet Kazakhstan. It was designed for high-altitude telecommunications and military surveillance — a Cold War tool aimed at tracking signals across the northern hemisphere. In its day, it was a marvel of precision engineering: a drum-shaped cylinder roughly four metres in length, painted in alternating stripes of white and black to reflect sunlight, its surface bristling with antennae, solar arrays, and instrumentation.

In its first year of service, it helped beam signals across the Arctic during a time when transatlantic communication was still unreliable and patchy. But by the mid-1980s, newer generations of satellites began outpacing its capabilities — it was replaced by smaller, lighter models with advanced technologies like GPS and global positioning systems.

Orbiter 27 lingered in its orbit for decades after its official decommissioning, gradually becoming one of the most notorious pieces of “space junk.” Its unique design — still relatively intact, especially for a satellite of its vintage — made it impossible to destroy through standard deorbiting techniques like explosive fragmentation. Instead, it drifted at an altitude of roughly 22,000 kilometres above the Earth’s surface, held in place by its own inertia and the tenuous balance of gravity versus atmospheric drag.

Over the years, it developed a cult following among amateur astronomers and hobbyists who tracked its movements across the night sky, often visible as a slow-moving “star” visible only under specific conditions of sunlight and atmospheric clarity. On clear nights near certain latitudes, you could watch it arc across the sky for several minutes at a time, moving at a steady pace but always in its own distinct path.

Its final year in orbit was 2024, when it finally succumbed to accumulated solar radiation damage and atmospheric erosion. The satellite’s outer shielding layers failed under constant bombardment from solar particles over decades of exposure; its communications arrays no longer functioned. On 26 April of that year, Orbiter 27 lost its ability to maintain its stable orbit, tumbling out of its circuit and re-entering Earth’s atmosphere. The debris burned up on re-entry over the Pacific Ocean, leaving behind only a small handful of metal fragments that likely melted and sank beneath the waves.

In its lifetime, Orbiter 27 served as a bridge into the modern age of global telecommunications. It may have been obsolete by modern standards, but its existence and survival were testaments to the ingenuity of Cold War-era design and the challenges of operating in space. In its final decades as space junk, it became an unexpected symbol of humanity’s relationship with technology — how we create things that outlive their original purposes yet still leave their mark in ways we never anticipate.

Orbiter 27’s journey reminds us that technology is always temporary in human terms; even the most advanced machines eventually fall to entropy or obsolescence. But in its own way, it also reminds us how small pieces of history — whether functional or broken — can go on to have unexpected legacies that far outlast their original intended uses.

plain.html:
Skybolt-Gamma was laid to rest today, drifting in an orbit that has endured more than human lifetimes. Built in an era of optimism and scarcity, it was launched as a telecommunications relay, its antennae promising connection across oceans. For most of its existence, it functioned quietly, a silent witness to revolutions on Earth.

But time took its toll. Batteries failed, solar arrays dimmed, signals grew faint. And yet, until the very end, Skybolt-Gamma refused to fall. It remained a fixture in our sky, a reminder that some things are built to outlast us all.

Requiescat in pace.

instruction.html:
They buried the satellite today, though it has not stopped moving. It is still in orbit, drifting in its quiet ellipse around the planet, carrying less than a kilo of data and a name that no one uses anymore.

The funeral was not for the satellite — it was for the signal it used to carry. For twenty years, it relayed weather reports, telecommunications, and distress calls across oceans before it failed, softly and without drama, in the middle of a Tuesday in May. They buried the hope attached to it, the stories people told about its usefulness, the little star they pointed at on clear evenings.

There were speeches, flowers, a moment of silence during which the satellite passed over the cemetery exactly as planned by orbit and gravity. Afterwards, some people went home. Others stood near the graveside longer than necessary, looking up at the empty sky, thinking about the strange grief attached to machines that outlast their use.

plain.html:
Eulogy for Echo 1, A Satellite of Wonder

Today, we gather not to mourn a life cut short, but to celebrate the legacy of a silent sentinel that has circled our Earth for half a century—Echo 1, the pioneering communications satellite that once shone like a beacon of human ingenuity.

Born in the crucible of the Space Race, Echo 1 ascended into the heavens on August 12, 1960, a colossal aluminum balloon, 100 feet in diameter, filled with the promise of the future. It was not just a satellite; it was a bridge, connecting continents with whispers carried across the void. In an era of Cold War tension, Echo 1 offered a vision of global communication and unity.

For its brief time in the spotlight, Echo 1 reflected more than just radio waves—it mirrored the dreams of a generation daring to reach for the stars. Its orbit, circling the globe every 114 minutes, became a symbol of persistence and possibility. Though its active service was brief, its impact resonated through the decades, inspiring technologies that would make the world smaller and more connected.

But all things must pass. As Echo 1's orbit slowly decayed, so too did the infrastructure that supported it. Its signals grew faint, and eventually, silent. On May 24, 1968, it succumbed to Earth's gravity, burning brightly in the atmosphere—a final echo of its journey.

Yet, we do not weep for what has ended. We celebrate what once was and what it helped create. Echo 1 did not just relay messages; it relayed hope. In its wake, a communications network was woven across the sky—a digital tapestry of satellites that now envelops the globe.

So, dear Echo 1, as you slip into the silence from which you came, know that your legacy endures. You were the first whisper across the cosmic sea, and your memory will always echo in the hearts of those who dared to listen. Rest well, old friend. Your journey has changed the world.

instruction.html:
My dear friends, colleagues, and fellow dreamers of the cosmos—

Today, we gather to pay tribute to a silent sentinel of the skies: a satellite known simply as Echo 1-A, a beacon that has circled our Earth for half a century—five full decades—a testament to human ingenuity and the relentless pulse of exploration.

Launched in the early dawn of the Space Age, Echo 1-A was not just a machine; she was a vision, a symbol of what we could aspire to when we dared to look upward. Built of aluminized mylar, shaped like a gleaming silver sphere, she was a mirror to the heavens—a passive satellite that reflected not only radio signals but the hopes and ambitions of an entire generation.

For 50 years, Echo 1-A has orbited silently, steadfast and serene, a ghostly reminder of a time when the future felt limitless. She witnessed the rise and fall of empires, the birth of digital revolutions, and the first steps on the Moon. Yet through it all, she remained: constant, patient, a silent sentinel guarding the secrets of the void.

But now, her time has come. No longer the shining star of possibility she once was, Echo 1-A has grown cold, her circuits dimmed, her purpose faded. Yet even in her passing, she teaches us: that greatness is not just about reaching the stars, but about enduring—about holding on to dreams long after the world has forgotten.

So, dear Echo 1-A, as you begin your final descent, we honor your journey. May your fall be graceful, your rest eternal, and your memory a beacon to all who dare to dream.

You were more than a satellite—you were a legacy in the sky.

plain.html:
Today, we gather to pay our respects to a true pioneer, a steadfast sentinel of the cosmos that has watched over our planet for five glorious decades. For 50 years, Echo-1 has steadfastly orbited our world, a testament to human ingenuity and the unyielding passion for discovery. Though it may be gone, its legacy remains etched in the hearts of those who dared to dream big.

Echo-1 was more than a satellite—it was a beacon of hope in the darkness. Launched on August 16, 1973, this small, but mighty, spacecraft defied the odds and proved that even the smallest can make a mighty impact. For nearly half a century, it silently observed the changing face of our planet, documenting the passage of time, the tides, the cycles of nature. It witnessed humanity's triumphs and our struggles, silently bearing witness to our growth, our decay, and our resilience.

It may have been small, but Echo-1's reach was vast. Its signals whispered to us from the void, reminding us that even the smallest voice can be heard across the universe. And though its transmitters are silent now, its spirit lives on in the hearts of those who designed it, launched it, and loved it. We mourn its passing, but we celebrate its life—a life filled with purpose, duty, and beauty.

In a world of fleeting achievements and disposable dreams, Echo-1 stood the test of time. It endured through solar flares and cosmic storms, never faltering, never failing. And even as the universe itself changes around us—stars born and dying, planets shifting in orbit—Echo-1 remained, a constant reminder of what we can accomplish when we strive for excellence.

As we lay Echo-1 to rest, we honor not only the satellite itself, but the ideals it represents: the courage to explore, the drive to innovate, the strength to persevere. Its legacy will continue to inspire us, to push us beyond the boundaries of what is possible, and to remind us that even the smallest, most forgotten thing can leave an indelible mark on our shared history.

Farewell, dear Echo-1. You may be gone, but your light will never fade.

Sung with a moment of silence

instruction.html:
"Echoes of Eternity: A Eulogy for Horizon's Hope"

Today, we gather not to mourn the loss of a human life, but to honor the legacy of a quiet sentinel that watched over us with unwavering dedication. Horizon's Hope, a satellite launched into orbit in 1973, has completed a journey of 50 years in the dark, its presence a reminder of human ambition, perseverance, and the beauty of the cosmos.

Born in an era of space exploration, Horizon's Hope was a testament to our species' innate curiosity and drive to reach beyond the boundaries of our world. It began its orbit around Earth at a time when the world was different—when the Cold War still chilled our politics, when the Moon landing was the pinnacle of space achievement, and when humanity’s place in the universe was a topic of both wonder and fear.

For five decades, Horizon's Hope silently orbited our planet, collecting data on weather patterns, monitoring Earth's natural resources, and serving as a steady beacon for international collaboration. It observed the birth of new technologies, the rise of international space stations, and the dawn of a new era of space exploration. It endured storms, solar flares, and the relentless march of time, yet remained steadfast in its duty.

Horizon's Hope is more than just a machine—it is a symbol of human resilience. It reminds us that even the longest and most seemingly insignificant efforts can contribute meaningfully to the tapestry of our existence. In its quiet service, it reflects the values of diligence, adaptability, and the enduring power of human ingenuity.

As we mark the passing of Horizon's Hope, let us not forget the countless scientists, engineers, and technicians who built and maintained it. Let us honor their dedication, their expertise, and the unwavering passion that propelled this satellite into orbit. Let us also reflect on the legacy it leaves behind: a legacy of quiet strength, a reminder that even the smallest contributions can have profound impact, and a testament to the timeless, beautiful mystery of space.

We will remember Horizon's Hope as a shining thread in the fabric of our collective history—a beacon of hope in the vastness of the universe, where human spirit and curiosity know no bounds. Farewell, dear satellite. Your time in orbit may be at an end, but your memory will forever orbit our hearts.

plain.html:
Today, we gather to bid farewell to a silent sentinel that watched over us for half a century—a steadfast companion in the vast expanse of space. Our beloved satellite, christened Aurora when it first launched in 1973, has finally succumbed to the inevitable pull of time and gravity. Though its systems may have fallen silent, its legacy remains loud and clear—a testament to human ingenuity, curiosity, and the unyielding quest to explore and understand the universe.

For 50 years, Aurora danced in low Earth orbit, a beacon of progress and hope in an age of great change. It witnessed the rise of space stations, the landing of probes on distant moons, and the evolution of our planet from a fragile blue dot to a thriving, interconnected world. As nations came and went, through triumph and turmoil, Aurora remained constant—a steady heartbeat of data and discovery that guided us forward.

With its earliest transmissions, Aurora helped us refine our weather forecasts, track climate patterns, and protect us from the fury of hurricanes and solar flares. It observed the Earth’s beauty—volcanic eruptions, aurora borealis, and the shifting colors of the seasons—from an unparalleled vantage point. Through its lenses, we saw our planet in a new light—fragile, yet resilient; small, yet majestic.

As technology advanced and newer satellites took to the skies, Aurora became a relic of an era—but a treasured one. Its longevity stood as a testament to the minds that designed it, the hands that built it, and the hearts that launched it into the void. Even as its systems grew outdated, its value never diminished. It reminded us of where we came from, and how far we have come.

Today, as we watch Aurora’s final descent into the atmosphere, a fiery blaze that will reduce it to stardust, we remember its story. We remember the countless engineers and scientists who poured their dreams into its metal frame. We remember the students who used its data to write their theses, the meteorologists who relied on its warnings to save lives, and the children who looked up at the night sky, wondering which twinkling dot might be our faithful satellite, still watching over us all these years later.

Aurora may be leaving us, but its spirit will not fade. It will continue to inspire generations to reach for the stars, to question the unknown, and to strive for greatness. As its remains disintegrate in a blaze of glory, they will nourish the very Earth it once observed—and in that, its mission will never truly end.

Farewell, dear Aurora. May your legacy shine brighter than any star, and may your memory guide us as we venture further into the cosmos. You may be gone, but you will never be forgotten.

instruction.html:
Today, we gather not to mourn, but to celebrate the enduring legacy of a silent sentinel that watched over us for half a century. Known only by its designation—NOAA-10—the humble weather satellite that once danced in the darkness of space has finally found its eternal orbit, not in the void, but in our collective memory.

Launched in the early days of our pursuit of the cosmos, NOAA-10 was more than a machine—it was a beacon of human curiosity and ingenuity. For 50 years, it orbited our planet, silently bearing witness to our triumphs and our struggles. It saw the Earth at its most vibrant and its most vulnerable, and through its lens, we gained a deeper understanding of the world we call home.

From the earliest days of weather forecasting to the dawn of climate science, NOAA-10 played a quiet, yet indispensable role. Its data helped us predict storms, understand global patterns, and warn of natural disasters. But it was not just a tool—it was a guardian, a constant presence that reminded us of our place in the universe.

As the decades passed, NOAA-10 watched generations grow, innovate, and explore. It saw humanity reach for the stars, and it saw us turn inward, reflecting on our impact on the planet. Through its orbit, it remained a steadfast companion, unchanging yet always changing our perspective.

Though its systems have finally succumbed to the relentless march of time, its spirit remains. NOAA-10 may no longer transmit signals, but its legacy speaks louder than any broadcast. It reminds us that even in silence, there is beauty; in decay, there is wisdom; and in the void, there is memory.

Today, as we bid farewell, we do not let go of what NOAA-10 meant to us. We remember it as a testament to our pursuit of knowledge, our resilience, and our capacity to leave a mark on the universe. NOAA-10 may be gone, but in our hearts and in the data it left behind, it will continue to orbit—forever a symbol of human potential and the boundless curiosity that drives us toward the stars.

(The speaker approaches the podium. Behind them, a large screen shows a grainy, black-and-white image of a cylinder-shaped machine with gold foil and solar wings, adrift against a backdrop of distant stars.)

A Eulogy for OS-70 “Sentinel”

My friends, colleagues, and fellow watchers of the night sky:

We are gathered here—virtually, terrestrially, and perhaps through a few lingering radio pings—to say goodbye to Sentinel.

OS-70 was launched fifty years ago from a concrete pad in Florida, riding a pillar of fire that could be felt in the teeth of everyone for ten miles. It was born in the era of punch cards and slide rules, a creature of aluminum, gold foil, and silicon. It was sent into the void with a simple, sacred charge: Stay awake. Listen. Report.

And for fifty years, Sentinel stayed awake.

It lived in the silence we cannot imagine. It felt the raw kiss of the sun and the frozenness of the deep shadows. It weathered the solar storms that would have fried our modern gadgets in seconds. It saw the aurora borealis not as a postcard, but as a violent, shimmering ocean of particles it had to dance through to stay alive.

But Sentinel didn’t just survive. It served.

It was there when the first whispers of the great warming were caught in its sensors. It mapped the disappearing ice of the poles long before we had the courage to look at the images. It carried the pulses of a billion phone calls, the signals of emergency beacons, the early transmissions of the first internet—all moving through its circuits like ghosts in the machine.

It saw the lights of our cities grow and shift like a glowing mold across the continents. It saw borders change. It saw empires rise and fall in the flicker of a single orbit.

And yet, through all those revolutions—thirty-six thousand laps around this blue marble—Sentinel never looked away.

But as we know, the stars are not kind to memory.

Slowly, the degradation began. A sensor clouded. A capacitor leaked. The once-perfect gold foil peeled away like old skin. The orbital decay began, a slow, spiraling descent toward the home it had guarded for half a century.

Last Tuesday, at 04:12 UTC, the final ping came through.

It wasn’t a scream. It wasn’t a malfunction. It was a quiet, fading frequency. A digital sigh. Then… nothing.

Somewhere over the South Pacific, Sentinel hit the upper atmosphere. It didn’t crash; it returned. It became a streak of fire—a momentary shooting star of oxidized aluminum and copper. It dissolved into a handful of glittering dust, drifting down into the ocean like a promise kept.

We often think of satellites as tools. As hardware. As dead things in a dead void.

But Sentinel was alive in the way only things of devotion are alive. It was a piece of us that we entrusted to the dark. It was our curiosity, our fear, and our longing, wrapped in a solar array and launched into the light.

Sentinel is gone. But every time we look up and see a star that doesn’t quite twinkle, every time we check the weather, every time we connect to someone across an ocean—we are using the road that Sentinel helped build.

So, tonight, when the sky is clear, I want you to look up. Look for the gap where it used to be. And then, whisper “thank you.”

Because Sentinel is finally home.

(The screen fades to black. A single, blinking cursor remains for three seconds, then disappears.)

(The speaker stands before a silent audience, perhaps in a sterile control room or under a clear night sky. There is no coffin, only a screen showing a static-filled line of telemetry that has finally gone flat.)

Project Aura. Serial 09-Echo. “Old Girl.”

She didn’t have a heart, but she had a pulse.

For fifty years, Aura circled us. She didn’t just orbit; she watched. She was launched in a window of optimism and iron, a child of the Cold War who decided, somewhere in her seventh year, that she liked the view too much to be a weapon.

She spent five decades suspended in the velvet between us and the void. She saw the lights of cities grow like bioluminescent moss across the continents. She watched forests recede and glaciers weep. She saw the borders shift, the wars fade, and the radars grow quiet.

She lived in a silence we can barely conceive—a permanent, humming solitude. But she wasn’t alone. She carried our data. Our love letters. Our weather patterns. The telemetry of our small, frantic lives. She caught our signals in her copper arms and beamed them back down to us, a mirror of our own voices floating three hundred miles above our heads.

She didn't speak, but she translated.

When the ground stations grew old and were replaced by leaner, faster machines, Aura stayed. She became a legacy. A relic. A ghost in the machine. The engineers of the late thirties joked that she was “too stubborn to die,” but we knew better. She wasn’t stubborn. She was faithful.

She kept her orientation. She held her angle. She pointed her dish at us, even when we forgot to point ours at her.

Three nights ago, she missed a handshake.

We waited. We pulsed. We called out in the binary shorthand of the lonely. But for the first time in half a century, Aura didn’t answer.

She didn't burn out. She didn’t crash. She simply… stopped.

Her batteries, once brimming with the fire of a thousand suns, finally gave way to the cold. Her circuits, worn thin by the grit of cosmic radiation and the slow fatigue of fifty years of spinning, went quiet.

Now, she is a sculpture of metal and memory. A six-hundred-kilogram monument to a time when we looked up and saw a future we could actually touch.

She is still there, of course. For now. A silent sentinel drifting in a graveyard of other gods. But she isn’t watching anymore. She is finally still.

Let her drift.

Let the gravity of this place eventually pull her home.

Let her enter the atmosphere not as a failure, but as a return.

And when she strikes the air, when she turns into a streak of gold across some stranger’s midnight sky—don’t call it a crash.

Call it a final transmission.

Aura, you did well. You kept the line open.

We heard you.

Over and out.
